opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the central weirdness of quantum mechanics, and I like to put it as bluntly as I can. Quantum mechanics has two rules that, on their face, look like they have nothing to do with each other.

The first rule is how an isolated system evolves when nobody's looking. There, the state is a vector of complex numbers called amplitudes, one for each possible configuration, and it changes by a unitary transformation. That evolution is completely deterministic and completely reversible. There's no randomness at all. If you know the state now, Schrödinger's equation tells you exactly what it'll be later, and you could in principle run it backwards. It's linear algebra, just with complex numbers instead of ordinary probabilities.

The second rule is what happens when you measure. Suddenly the system "collapses" to one definite outcome, and the probability of each outcome is the squared absolute value of its amplitude. That's the Born rule. And that step is random, irreversible, and nonlinear. All the probability in quantum mechanics enters at that moment and nowhere else.

The way I often explain it is that quantum mechanics is like probability theory, but with minus signs. In classical probability, the numbers are nonnegative, so different paths to the same outcome can only add up. With amplitudes, which can be negative or complex, paths can cancel each other out. That's interference, and it's the whole source of quantum computing's power: you try to choreograph things so that the amplitudes for wrong answers cancel and the amplitudes for the right answer reinforce, all while the system evolves unitarily. Then you measure, and only then do you roll the dice.

Now, the obvious question is: what counts as a measurement? A measuring device is itself made of atoms that should obey the first rule. That's the measurement problem, and that's where the interpretations split. Many-worlds says there's only unitary evolution, and the apparent randomness is just your uncertainty about which branch you're in after you become entangled with the system. Copenhagen-style views treat measurement as a primitive. Bohmian mechanics adds hidden variables. Collapse theories like GRW say unitarity really does break down at some scale, which in principle you could test experimentally.

What I find striking is that, to whatever extent we understand it, decoherence explains why we never see interference between macroscopically distinct outcomes. Once information about a system leaks out into the environment, the branches effectively stop talking to each other. That's why quantum computers are so hard to build: you have to keep the system isolated enough to stay in the deterministic, unitary regime. But decoherence by itself doesn't tell you why you experience one particular outcome with Born-rule probabilities. That last step is where physics hands off to philosophy, and honestly, I don't think anyone has closed that gap to everyone's satisfaction.

r001.rationale: It says measurement is where the Born-rule probabilities enter and states, “All the probability in quantum mechanics enters at that moment and nowhere else.”

r002.rationale: It says an isolated system evolves by a unitary transformation and that this evolution is “completely deterministic.”

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the way I'd put it is that quantum mechanics really has two very different kinds of rules in it, and the whole conceptual weirdness of the theory comes from how they sit next to each other.

The first rule is about what happens to an isolated system when nobody's looking at it. And that part is completely deterministic. You have a state, which is this vector of amplitudes, these complex numbers, and it evolves according to the Schrödinger equation, which is just a linear, reversible, unitary transformation. There's no randomness anywhere in that. If you tell me the state now, I can tell you the state a second from now, exactly. And crucially, it's reversible, so I can also run it backwards and tell you the state a second ago. Nothing is ever lost.

The second rule is the measurement rule, the Born rule. That's the one that says: when you look at the system, you see one outcome, and the probability of each outcome is the squared absolute value of its amplitude. And this rule is the only place where probability enters the theory at all. It's also, not coincidentally, the only place where irreversibility enters. Once you've measured, the other branches are gone as far as you're concerned, and you can't undo that.

So one way to say it is: amplitudes are the thing that evolves, and probabilities are the thing you get when you cash amplitudes out by looking. And the reason amplitudes aren't just probabilities in disguise is that they can be negative, or complex, and so they can interfere. Two paths to the same outcome can cancel each other out. Probabilities can't do that. Probabilities only ever add. So the time evolution part of the theory genuinely isn't a story about an ignorant observer who's missing some information; it's a different kind of mathematical object doing something probabilities fundamentally can't.

Now, the obvious question, and this has been the obvious question for a hundred years, is: why are there two rules? Measurement is presumably just a physical process, your measuring apparatus is made of atoms, so shouldn't it also just obey the Schrödinger equation? And if you take that seriously, you get something like the many-worlds picture, where the "collapse" is really just you getting entangled with the system and becoming part of one branch. Or you can say no, collapse is a real, additional physical event, and then you owe me a story about exactly when and how it happens. Or you take the operational view and say the theory is a tool for predicting outcomes of measurements, full stop, and stop asking.

I don't think any of those is obviously right. But I think the cleanest thing you can say, without picking a side, is exactly the distinction you asked about: there's a deterministic, reversible, linear evolution of amplitudes, and there's a probabilistic, irreversible readout rule, and the entire interpretation debate is basically a fight about whether the second thing is fundamental or whether it's somehow emergent from the first.

r001.rationale: It says the Born measurement rule is “the only place where probability enters the theory at all,” clearly conveying the criterion in the quantum-mechanics context.

r002.rationale: It states that an isolated system evolves deterministically according to the Schrödinger equation.

astra-6.text:
Well, there are two different rules here. When an isolated quantum system evolves over time, its quantum state evolves deterministically, according to the Schrödinger equation. If you know the initial state and the forces acting on it, you can predict the later state exactly. That’s called unitary evolution.

Probability enters when you make a measurement. The state assigns an amplitude to each possible outcome, and the Born rule says that the probability of an outcome is the squared absolute value of its amplitude. So you can predict the probabilities exactly, but generally you can’t predict which individual outcome you’ll see.

The crucial thing is that amplitudes aren’t ordinary probabilities. They can be positive, negative, or complex, and they can interfere—reinforcing or canceling one another. That interference happens during the deterministic evolution. Measurement is where those amplitudes translate into probabilities for what we observe.

Now, how those two rules fit together is the measurement problem, and different interpretations tell different stories about it. But that distinction—deterministic evolution of the quantum state versus probabilistic measurement outcomes—is the standard operational picture.

r001.rationale: The response says probability enters upon measurement and contrasts that with deterministic evolution, framing this as the standard operational picture.

r002.rationale: It explicitly states that an isolated quantum system evolves deterministically according to the Schrödinger equation.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, there are two different rules here. If you have an isolated quantum system, its state evolves deterministically according to the Schrödinger equation. That evolution is unitary. So if you know the initial state and the dynamics, you can calculate exactly what the state will be later. There’s no randomness in that rule.

Probability enters when you make a measurement. The state gives you amplitudes for the possible outcomes, and the Born rule says that the probability of each outcome is the squared absolute value of its amplitude. Even with complete knowledge of the state, you generally can’t predict which outcome you’ll see.

The subtlety is that a measuring apparatus is itself made of quantum stuff. So how these two descriptions fit together—deterministic evolution of the whole system and probabilistic outcomes for an observer—is the measurement problem. Different interpretations tell different stories about that, while largely agreeing on the probabilities we actually observe.

r001.rationale: The response says probability enters when a measurement is made, but does not clearly state that measurement is the only place probability enters known fundamental physics.
